newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch Stork pulls out of Fokker rescue - paper.
newsitem.headline: Dutch Stork pulls out of Fokker rescue - paper.

text.p: Dutch engineering firm Stork has pulled out of rescue talks for bankrupt planemaker Fokker NV fuelling speculation that lengthy efforts to save the aircraft pioneer may now collapse, Dutch daily de Telegraaf said on Saturday.

The paper, citing sources close to the talks, said Stork, one of four parties involved in protracted rescue negotiations for Fokker, had pulled out because the Malaysian government had refused to help finance start-up costs for a Fokker re-launch.

Two other Dutch parties, the government and Deleye Investment, a firm headed by the chairman of Dutch industrial investment group Begemann, will meet again on Monday to reconsider their options, Telegraaf said.
None of the parties was immediately available for comment on the Telegraaf report.

A team from the Malaysian state investment company Khazanah visited the Netherlands last month to discuss a rescue plan for Fokker, which has been run by court-appointed insolvency lawyers since it was declared bankrupt over a year ago.
After the Dutch parties agreed on March 13 a common position for negotiations with the Malaysians, it had been hoped that a deal could be struck by May 1.
Fokker was forced into bankruptcy last year when majority shareholder Daimler Benz AG of Germany pulled the plug, saying it could no longer bear Fokker's huge losses.
The "Malaysian option" was seen as the final lifeline for Fokker, one of the pioneering companies of European aviation.
Tentative rescue plans assumed the Malaysians would invest 450 million guilders ($237.3 million) in a new Fokker, the Dutch state 475 million, Stork 175 million and Deleye 25 million.
Dutch Economics Minister Hans Wijers last month warned against over-optimism, saying there would be no relaunch unless substantial foreign investment could be secured.
After Daimler abandoned Fokker, Stork bought the profitable Fokker aircraft maintenance and components businesses in a deal binding it to involvement in a relaunch.
